title: Multicore and Shared-Memory Multiprocessors
subtitle: Many cores, one memory, and the problems that creates.

objectives: Explain why processors moved to multiple cores
Compare centralized (UMA) and distributed (NUMA) shared memory
Explain the cache coherence problem and trace the MSI protocol
Explain a race condition and fix it with a lock
Describe atomic operations and apply Amdahl's Law to parallel speed-up

steps.question: Your laptop has 8 cores. Will a program run 8 times faster on it? And what happens when two cores change the same variable?
clues: More cores give more **peak** performance, but only if the **program is parallel**.
Cores share memory, so their **caches can disagree**.
Without care, two threads updating one variable **lose updates**.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: From faster cores to more cores

items: Clock speeds stopped rising about 2005 because of the **power wall** (Class 2)
ILP is limited by dependences and branches (Class 14)
So designers put **several cores** on one chip instead: a **multicore** processor
Programs must be written (or compiled) to use **many threads** to benefit

head: Uniprocessor
Multicore
rows: Parallelism in the program, memory and power

steps.why: Parallel hardware is the way performance is still growing, but it shifts the burden to software.
steps.real: Phones have 6 to 8 cores; servers have dozens to hundreds.

explainAgain.beginner: One very fast cook cannot get much faster, so you hire more cooks; but they need separate tasks and must not fight over the same pan.

steps.title: Amdahl's Law for parallel programs

terms.note: p = fraction that can run in parallel; n = number of cores

steps.why: The serial part of a program limits what any number of cores can achieve.
steps.real: A program that is 90% parallel can never go more than 10 times faster, however many cores it has.

mistake.wrong: Eight cores give eight times the speed.
mistake.right: Only if 100% of the work is parallel and there are no overheads.

steps.title: Calculate: parallel speed-up
steps.why: 90% parallel on 8 cores: 4.71 times, an efficiency of 59%, with a limit of 10. At 95% and 16 cores: 9.14.

steps.question: A program is 90% parallel and runs on 8 cores. What is the speed-up?
steps.result: The 10% serial part dominates as n grows.

steps.statement: Doubling the number of cores always doubles the speed of every program.
steps.why: Programs with serial parts or heavy synchronization gain much less.

steps.title: Shared memory

blocks.text: In a **shared-memory multiprocessor** every core can load and store the same **single address space**. Threads communicate simply by reading and writing shared variables. There are two main organisations.

steps.why: Programs see one memory, which makes programming easier, but the hardware organisation decides how fast each access is.
steps.real: Almost every laptop, phone and server processor is a shared-memory multiprocessor.

steps.title: Centralized shared memory (UMA)

steps.text: Several **cores**, each with its own **private cache**, on one chip or board.
The caches connect to a **shared bus** (or similar interconnect).
One **main memory** serves every core, and every core is the **same distance** from it: **uniform** memory access (UMA).

steps.why: One memory, one bus: simple, but the bus limits how many cores can be added.

steps.title: Follow reads in the UMA design

steps.text: The complete organisation. Choose a scenario and press Play or Step.
Core 0 looks in its private cache first.
On a miss the request goes over the shared bus to the single main memory.
Core 3 looks in its private cache.
The same bus and memory serve it, with the same latency as core 0. The bus can become the bottleneck as cores are added.

steps.why: Both cores see the same memory latency: uniform memory access.

steps.title: Distributed shared memory (NUMA)

steps.text: Each **node** has a core with its cache and its **own local memory**.
The nodes are connected by a **network**. All memories together form one **shared address space**.

steps.why: Memory is spread over the nodes, so each core has a fast local memory and a slower view of the rest.

steps.title: Local and remote accesses

steps.text: The complete organisation. Choose a scenario and press Play or Step.
The data is in core 0's own memory: a **fast local access**.
The data lives in node 3's memory: the request leaves node 0 and crosses the network.
Node 3 returns the data. A **remote access** takes much longer: **non-uniform** memory access (NUMA).

steps.why: Remote accesses cross the network and take longer: non-uniform memory access.

steps.title: Comparing the two

head: Centralized (UMA)
Distributed (NUMA)
rows: Limited by the bus and memory (a few to tens of cores)
Software should place data near the threads that use it

steps.why: UMA is simpler but does not scale; NUMA scales but exposes the memory distance to software.
steps.real: Dual-socket servers are NUMA machines: each CPU socket has its own DRAM.

mistake.wrong: NUMA means the memory is not shared.
mistake.right: It is still one address space; only the access times differ.

steps.question: What does UMA stand for and mean?
options: Uniform memory access: every core sees the same latency to memory
Unordered memory access: loads may be reordered
steps.why: In UMA all cores reach the single memory at the same cost.

steps.title: The coherence problem

items: Each core has a **private cache** holding copies of memory
Core 0 changes variable x in its cache; core 1 still holds the **old** x
Core 1 reads a **stale** value: the caches are **incoherent**
A coherent system makes every read return the **latest write**

steps.why: Without coherence, shared memory would give different cores different answers for the same variable.
steps.real: Coherence is maintained entirely by hardware, invisible to the programmer.

explainAgain.beginner: Two people keep the same shopping list on their own phones; if one adds milk and the other never sees it, they buy twice.

steps.title: The MSI protocol (simplified)

head: State
Meaning
rows: This is the only copy and it has been changed; memory is stale
A clean copy; other caches may also have it
No valid copy in this cache

items: A **write** invalidates every other copy (the others go to I)
A **read miss** fetches the value; if another cache holds it in M, that cache writes it back first
Caches **snoop** the bus to see each other's requests

steps.why: These three states and the rule "a write invalidates the other copies" are enough to keep all caches coherent.
steps.real: Real processors use MESI or MOESI variants; the idea is the same.

deeper.text: Directory-based protocols replace snooping on large (NUMA) machines.

steps.title: Try it: with and without coherence

blocks.title: Two cores sharing x
blocks.hint: First turn the protocol **OFF**: have core 0 and core 1 read x, then let core 0 write; read on core 1 and look for the stale value. Then switch it ON and repeat.

steps.why: With the protocol OFF core 1 keeps reading its old copy of x. With MSI ON, core 0's write invalidates core 1's copy and the next read gets the new value.

steps.title: A trace
steps.why: Every write invalidates the other copy, and every read after a write gets the latest value from the owner.
steps.real: A write to a Shared line is called an upgrade; a read of a Modified line forces a write-back.

steps.question: Both cores hold x in state S. Core 0 writes x. What are the states afterwards?

reveal.text: The write invalidates core 1's copy: **core 0 = M, core 1 = I**. Memory is now stale until core 0's block is written back.

steps.result: Core 1's next read will fetch the new value from core 0.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about coherence is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. A write invalidates other caches' copies.
2. A line in state M is the only valid copy, and memory is stale.
3. Coherence is maintained by the programmer inserting special instructions on every write.
4. Caches snoop the bus to see other cores' requests.
steps.explain: Coherence is handled by hardware; the programmer does not add instructions for it.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why does a write have to invalidate the other cores' copies instead of just updating them?
steps.answer: Invalidating needs only one short bus message and then further writes by the same core are free (state M, no bus traffic). Updating every copy on every write would flood the bus. The cost is that other cores take a miss if they read the line again.

steps.title: Race conditions

blocks.text: Two threads each execute **counter = counter + 1** on a shared variable. In machine terms it is three steps: **load**, **add**, **store**.

steps.why: Both threads read the old value, so one increment is lost: the final value is 1, not 2. The result depends on the timing: a **race condition**.
steps.real: Races cause the nastiest bugs: they appear rarely and vanish when you add debugging output.

mistake.wrong: Incrementing one variable is a single, safe operation.
mistake.right: It is a load, an add and a store; another thread can run between them.

steps.title: Try it: a lost update

blocks.title: Two threads, one counter
blocks.hint: Press **Try the bad interleaving** to see the lost update, then switch to **Using a lock** and try again. You can also step the threads yourself.

steps.why: The bad schedule ends with the counter at 1. With a lock the second thread must wait, and the counter is always 2.

steps.question: Two threads each add 1 to a counter that starts at 0 without any lock. Which final values are possible?

reveal.text: If one thread finishes before the other starts the result is **2**; if their load, add, store steps interleave badly one update is lost and the result is **1**.

steps.result: That unpredictability is the signature of a race condition.

steps.title: Locks

items: A **lock** lets only one thread at a time execute a **critical section** (the code that touches the shared data)
**lock**: wait until it is free, then take it; **unlock**: release it
With the lock, the load, add and store of one thread run as a unit
The price: threads **wait**, so too much locking removes the parallelism (Amdahl again)

steps.why: Locks make a sequence of steps look like one indivisible operation.
steps.real: Java's synchronized blocks and C++ mutexes are locks.

mistake.wrong: A lock makes the program faster.
mistake.right: It makes the program correct; it costs time because of the waiting.

steps.title: Atomic operations

items: How is a lock itself implemented without a race? With an **atomic** hardware operation
**Test-and-set** (or swap): read the old value and write 1 in one indivisible step; if the old value was 0 the lock was free and now belongs to you
**Load-linked / store-conditional (ll / sc)**: ll reads a value; sc stores only if nobody else wrote the location since the ll, and tells you whether it succeeded
An atomic operation cannot be interrupted by another core

blocks.code:
try:  ll   $t0, 0($s1)     # load-linked: read the counter
      addi $t0, $t0, 1     # add 1
      sc   $t0, 0($s1)     # store-conditional: $t0 = 1 if it worked, 0 if not
      beq  $t0, $zero, try # somebody interfered: try again

steps.why: Atomic instructions are the hardware foundation of locks, counters and lock-free data structures.
steps.real: MIPS and RISC-V use ll/sc (RISC-V calls them lr/sc); x86 uses atomic read-modify-write instructions.

deeper.text: The ll/sc loop turns "load, add, store" into an atomic increment without any lock.

steps.question: What does a failed store-conditional (sc) mean?
options: Another core wrote the location after the ll, so the update must be retried
steps.why: sc succeeds only if nothing wrote the location since the ll.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Put these steps of a correct locked increment in order.
items: Acquire the lock (wait if it is held)
Load the counter into a register
Add 1
Store the register to the counter
Release the lock
steps.why: The whole load-add-store sits between acquire and release.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Is it better to lock the whole data structure or each small piece of it?
ideas: One big lock is simple but serializes all threads (poor scaling).
Many small locks allow more parallelism but are harder to get right (deadlock risk).
Atomic operations avoid locks for simple counters.
The right choice depends on how much contention there is.

questions.a: A result that depends on the timing of threads accessing shared data.

questions.q: Why does a write invalidate other caches' copies?
questions.a: So no core can read a stale value.
From an atomic instruction such as test-and-set or ll/sc.

steps.question: Contrast UMA and NUMA in one sentence each.
steps.answer: UMA: all cores reach one memory with the same latency. NUMA: memory is distributed, so local accesses are fast and remote ones slow.
steps.solution: The difference is whether memory access time depends on where the data is.

steps.question: A program is 90% parallel. What is the speed-up on 8 cores and what is the limit?
Both cores hold x in state S (value 0). Core 0 writes 1. Give both states and memory; then core 1 reads x.
steps.answer: After the write: core 0 M(1), core 1 I, memory 0 (stale). After the read: both S(1), memory 1.
steps.solution: The write invalidates core 1; the read forces core 0 to write back and both become Shared.

steps.question: Trace MSI for two cores: (1) core 0 reads x, (2) core 1 reads x, (3) core 0 writes 1, (4) core 1 reads x, (5) core 1 writes 2, (6) core 0 reads x. Give the states and the value in memory after each.
steps.answer: 1: S,I; 0. 2: S,S; 0. 3: M(1),I; 0 stale. 4: S,S (1); memory 1. 5: I,M(2); memory 1 stale. 6: S,S (2); memory 2.
steps.solution: Each read miss loads the latest value; each write on a Shared line invalidates the other copy; a read of a Modified line writes it back.
steps.mistake: Leaving the old copy valid after a write.
steps.title: Exam practice: trace

steps.question: Two threads each execute load, add, store on a counter that starts at 0. Thread 0 loads, thread 1 loads, thread 0 adds and stores, thread 1 adds and stores. What is the final counter and why? How does a lock fix it?
steps.answer: Final counter = 1 (a lost update). With a lock the second thread cannot load until the first has stored and released, so the result is always 2.
steps.solution: Both threads loaded 0, so both stored 1. The lock makes load-add-store a critical section executed by one thread at a time.
steps.mistake: Saying the result is 2 because each thread adds 1.
steps.title: Exam practice: race

steps.question: A program is 95% parallel. Find the speed-up on 16 cores, on 100 cores, and the limit.
steps.mistake: Assuming speed-up equals the number of cores.
steps.title: Exam practice: Amdahl

steps.question: Explain why large multiprocessors use distributed shared memory (NUMA) instead of one centralized memory.
steps.answer: With one memory and one bus every core competes for the same bandwidth, so the bus becomes the bottleneck as cores are added. Distributing memory among the nodes gives each core its own fast local memory and spreads the traffic, so the machine scales to many more cores, at the cost of slower remote accesses and the need to place data near the threads that use it.
steps.solution: A strong answer mentions bandwidth and scalability and the local/remote difference.
steps.mistake: Saying NUMA memory is not shared.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: Clock speed and ILP stalled, so processors gained cores; programs must be parallel to benefit.
Amdahl's Law: speed-up = 1 ÷ ((1 − p) + p ÷ n); the serial part sets the limit.
UMA: one memory, equal latency; NUMA: local memory per node, fast local and slow remote.
Cache coherence: a write invalidates other copies; MSI = Modified, Shared, Invalid.
A race condition is a result that depends on thread timing; a lock makes a critical section atomic.
Atomic instructions (test-and-set, ll/sc) are the hardware basis of locks.

mistakes.wrong: More cores always mean proportionally more speed.
mistakes.right: The serial part and synchronization limit the gain.
It is load, add and store; another thread can interleave.
It is one address space with non-uniform access time.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Multicore processors appeared because clock speed and ILP stopped scaling. Shared-memory machines are centralized (UMA) or distributed (NUMA). Private caches need a coherence protocol such as MSI, in which a write invalidates other copies. When threads share data, race conditions lose updates; locks and atomic instructions such as test-and-set and ll/sc protect critical sections, and Amdahl's Law limits the speed-up.

questions.question: Why did processors move to multiple cores?
options: Clock speed and ILP stopped scaling because of power limits
questions.why: The power wall and limited ILP pushed designers to more cores.
questions.misconception: Multicore adds peak performance without a higher clock.

questions.statement: In MSI, a write invalidates the other caches' copies.
questions.why: That is how stale reads are prevented.
questions.misconception: The others go to state I.

questions.question: Which can protect a critical section?
questions.why: A lock allows one thread at a time.
questions.misconception: The others do not provide mutual exclusion.

questions.question: In NUMA, accessing the memory of another node is:
questions.misconception: That is why the access time is non-uniform.

questions.question: Both cores have x in S. Core 0 writes. States?
questions.why: The write invalidates the other copy.

questions.question: Two unsynchronized threads each add 1 to a counter starting at 0. A possible final value is:
questions.why: A lost update gives 1 (or 2 if no bad interleaving).

questions.question: What does the ll/sc pair do?
options: Performs an atomic update: sc fails if another core wrote the location after ll
questions.why: The store-conditional succeeds only if the location is unchanged since the load-linked.

items.a: Uniform memory access: one memory with equal latency for every core.
A result that depends on the timing of threads.

items.q: What implements a lock in hardware?
items.a: An atomic instruction such as test-and-set or ll/sc.
